problem: Existing EQA datasets are manually or rule-based built, have ambiguous non-unique answers, embed prior knowledge (so models answer without exploring), lack exploration trajectories, and their metrics measure only answer similarity, not grounding or exploration efficiency. Frontier-based exploration also struggles in cluttered scenes and lacks fine-grained exploration of task-relevant regions.
motivation: Agents can produce plausible but hallucinated or ungrounded answers that score well under similarity-based metrics, so exploration and reasoning ability are misjudged. Evaluating and improving EQA requires a benchmark with ground-truth exploration paths and unique answers, a metric that checks answer grounding in observations, and an explorer that focuses on task-relevant regions.
key_idea: Build an exploration-aware EQA benchmark (EXPRESS-Bench) with a grounding-aware metric (EAC), and a hybrid explorer (Fine-EQA) that switches between frontier-based and goal-oriented exploration over global and functional-region semantic maps.
insight: Grounding-aware scoring exposes hallucination: random exploration has a high ungrounded C* (62.75) but a low grounded C (36.95), whereas Fine-EQA reaches C 40.55. Ablating FBE or GOE lowers both accuracy and efficiency (w/o FBE: C 38.54, E_path 12.74; w/o GOE: C 39.63, E_path 14.64), so the two exploration modes are complementary. Multi-frame VLMs do worse than Socratic models, suggesting that extracting key information matters more than feeding many frames.
method: EXPRESS-Bench construction: sample start and target positions on the same floor in HM3D/Habitat (10-100 GT steps), record the shortest action sequence and first-person observations, generate open-ended QA from the final frame with GPT-4o-mini over 7 question types, then manually filter for uniqueness and scene relevance.

EAC metric: a VLM gives a correctness score σ (1-5) and a grounding score δ (0/0.5/1); C = mean(σδ/5), E_path additionally weights by path efficiency l/max(p,l), and d_T is the geodesic distance from the final position to the target.

Frontier-based exploration: build a 3D voxel map projected to 2D, sample points by farthest point sampling, obtain local (VLM-scored) and global (VLM confidence) semantic values, and update a Gaussian-smoothed semantic map; weight frontier candidates by semantic value, unexplored rate, unoccupied rate and distance decay, and sample the next frontier by these weights.

Functional region semantic map: the VLM classifies the current view into functional regions (kitchen, bedroom, ...) with a confidence threshold, and the map is updated around representative points; nearby same-ID points are merged into regions.

Goal-oriented exploration: an LLM (GPT-4) prioritizes regions relevant to the question, the global semantic map is masked to the highest-priority region, and the agent goes to the argmax point, decaying values of visited points; at most 3 consecutive explorations per region, then it returns to frontier exploration or the next region.
Stop and answer module: GPT-4o-mini judges at each step whether the current image suffices to answer (yes/no), and answers from the latest observation when it does.

setting.backbone: Prismatic VLM Prism-DINOSigLIP 7B (semantic values and region classification), GPT-4 (region prioritization), GPT-4o-mini (stop decision and answering), all frozen
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D with pose, four-direction views in designated regions
setting.action_space: waypoint/point selection within 3 m of the current position, executed by low-level navigation
setting.privileged: none for Fine-EQA (baselines like Socratic and Multi-Frame VLMs use GT trajectory frames)

numbers.eval_set_note: Fine-EQA on full question set; the OpenEQA GPT-4V baseline used a random 184-question subset
numbers.evidence: Table 'Performance comparison on the A-EQA subset of OpenEQA', Fine-EQA

numbers_note: EXPRESS-Bench and OpenEQA A-EQA are not canonical benchmark names, so they are given as 'other'. The split label 'test' is assumed because the paper does not name splits.
results: On EXPRESS-Bench, Fine-EQA obtains C 40.55, C* 63.95, E_path 16.22 and d_T 6.43, ahead of the RE, FBE and GOE agents (best baseline C 38.60 for FBE, E_path 14.55). All methods remain well below the human C* of 83.99. On A-EQA, Fine-EQA gets C' 43.27 and E' 29.16 versus 41.8 and 7.5 for OpenEQA with GPT-4V, and on HM-EQA it gets 56.0% accuracy with a 54.3 m path versus 50.4% and 93.7 m for Explore-EQA.
limitations: Relies on GPT-4o-mini/VLM for data generation, stop decisions and grounded scoring, so the metric and benchmark inherit VLM biases; the benchmark is simulator-only (HM3D) and was manually filtered.
Fine-EQA is weaker on existence and knowledge questions, and all agents remain far below human performance.
Comparisons with OpenEQA use different evaluation subsets (184 vs. full), and the Fine-EQA gains over the baselines are modest.
